item.title: Gen Z Is Driving Global Political Change, Aiding Far Left and Far Right
item.description:
Thousands of students are poised to hold simultaneous and coordinated protests in several European countries on Friday, demanding an end to war, to social-welfare spending cuts and, in some cases, to capitalism itself.

It is the latest iteration of the global youth uprisings that have spilled through streets from France to India this year, and helped to power recent election upsets across Europe and the Americas.

Polling shows that frustrated young people played a disproportionately large role in voting out nationalist leaders in Hungary and Serbia, in electing the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, and in putting a German far-right party on track to govern a German state for the first time since World War II. They could prove crucial in upcoming elections in France and Spain.

“It’s becoming harder and harder to not connect all of the different issues facing our generation,” said Adam Powell-Davies, 27, the national chair in Britain of the Socialist Students, one of the groups organizing Friday’s protests. “Not just in specific countries, but globally.”

The beneficiaries of this youth anger are ideologically diffuse. They include centrists — as well as insurgent politicians on the far left and on the far right who offer stark and social-media-friendly solutions to the ailments of an unsettled global order.

Organizers and experts say the connective tissue between these spasms of youth anger is a frustration with established political power structures, whatever their ideological bent — and a perception that economic opportunity is slipping away from young people.

A decade of pandemic, war, warming temperatures and a generation-defining fiscal reckoning in wealthy economies have combined to fuel fears that young people may never enjoy the peace, prosperity and freedoms of their parents and grandparents. Countries like France are struggling with high government debt and face difficult choices for how to maintain the promises of generous social welfare systems.

“There’s no future for us,” Laura Spearey, a 27-year-old information technology student from Bilbao, Spain, who traveled to Britain to join the Friday protests, said in an interview.

She cited difficulties in securing housing, health care and other necessities of adulthood: “You have no chance whatsoever to have your own life, to build your life project.”

Those anxieties have persisted for years: They also drove the “Occupy” protests that followed the 2008 financial crisis. But survey data suggests they are growing more urgent, even in countries, like Germany, where youth unemployment rates are still lower — and there is less government debt — than in Britain and France.

In Germany, young people’s economic concerns have grown in the past decade, according to “Youth in Germany,” an academic study that has surveyed more than 2,000 young people per year over nine years.

“The crucial question is not simply whether today’s young people are objectively worse off than previous generations,” said Klaus Hurrelmann, a professor of public health and education at Berlin’s Hertie School and a co-author of the “Youth in Germany” study. “What matters is that many of them are beginning to believe that the traditional promises of our society no longer apply to them.”

Across much of Europe, that belief has been further fueled by governments’ promises to spend more and more on national defense in the years to come, both to compensate for declining American military support for the continent and to counter threats from Russia. Younger protesters have called for a reversal of that buildup, saying it drains needed money for education, health care and other social services.

In Germany, many protests groups say they have been galvanized by government efforts to encourage young people to sign up for military service in an effort to bolster fighting forces, a move that many young people worry will lead to a military draft.

In a list of demands published ahead of Friday’s protests, one of the German groups organizing the events, “Gen Z Regelt” — roughly translated, “Gen Z Gets Things Done” — called for the resignation of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has taken the lead in ramping up German military spending. It also says “not one person, not one cent, for the German armed forces.”

The group’s demands, like the others behind Friday’s events, skew sharply to the left. They critique the capitalist system. They notably refrain from taking aim at older generations that have benefited from opportunities that they fear they are missing out on, like buying homes and securing generous pensions. Instead, they frame the conflict as workers versus the rich and powerful.

“It’s not a battle of the young versus the old,” said Hannah Ponting, 20, a member of the Socialist Students at Liverpool University, who is helping to coordinate protests there. “Neither of those groups are controlling where this money’s going.”

In Berlin in September, similar sentiments — and a surge of voting from people as young as 16 — helped the far-left party Die Linke score an upset victory in the city election.

In other parts of Europe and the world, though, the anxiety has driven young voters to the far right as well as the left.

According to recent polling in France, roughly one in five of voters aged under 25 says they will vote for the main far-right party in next year’s election, and an even higher proportion voted far-right in French legislative elections in 2024.

In the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, exit polls showed the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, won more than 40 percent of the youngest voters in a state election in September — more than double the share for any other party. The AfD’s main candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is a telegenic TikTok star who promised to restore opportunity for the state, by deporting some immigrants, providing new benefits to young parents and ending German support for Ukraine.

The success of the AfD and Die Linke in Germany illustrates how quickly young voters are willing to turn on political parties that promised rapid change but failed to deliver, said Mr. Hurrelmann of the Hertie School. Just five years ago, young Germans flocked to centrist parties in a national election.

The centrists have now lost out to the AfD and Die Linke, which have promised radical change by shunning the compromise-driven model of governance that has long dominated German life.

“They are completely free to promise everything,” Mr. Hurrelmann said, “because they are not now in a position to deliver.”

Mainstream parties have few incentives to meet young people’s demands, because doing so risks alienating the older voters who make up the majority of their coalitions, said Tim Vlandas, a professor at Oxford University who studies the political consequences of aging populations.

If the far left or far right were to take power, he added, they would likely face similar pressures — because they would also have to appeal to older generations to stay in government.

Such a cycle, he said, would just increase pressure on young people to take to the streets. “When you don’t influence politics, you can protest. You can become alienated and stop voting,” he said. Or, he added, “you can radicalize.”

item.title: Victims of Clerical Sexual Abuse Want More From Pope Leo
item.description:
Among the millions of people who looked forward to Pope Leo XIV’s visit to South America were survivors of clerical sexual abuse who hoped his presence might spur greater accountability for the abusers.

Instead, the trip, which concluded this week, has left them disappointed. They say the pope has not done enough to change the Roman Catholic Church’s approach to sexual abuse and lament how Leo met with only a relatively small number of victims, who were selected through a secretive process.

The frustration in South America reflected broader accusations throughout parts of the Catholic world that Leo, who was elected pope in May 2025, has not acted fast enough to ensure justice for victims or implement more safeguards to prevent future sexual abuse by priests. A papal commission that Pope Francis established in 2014 to develop protocols for protecting minors from clerical abuse presented its interim proposals to Leo this year, but the pontiff says that they need to be reviewed and finalized before being published.

“We haven’t seen him lift a single finger with the intention of changing anything within the Catholic Church’s system,” said José Enrique Escardó, the founder of a victims’ support group who said he was abused by members of an ultraconservative Catholic group disbanded by Pope Francis.

Leo, as a bishop in northern Peru, helped the group’s victims obtain mental health counseling and financial payments but, Mr. Escardó said, has not adequately built on that work as pontiff.

Leo has made “only pastoral statements, responses to journalists’ questions and staged meetings with victims,” Mr. Escardó said, adding that he wanted the pope to ensure that all abusers were prevented from serving in the church.

The Vatican declined to comment on the accounts and accusations in this article. Speaking publicly during the trip, Leo addressed the matter in general terms without outlining specific plans. He told bishops in Lima, Peru, that the Church must respond to clerical sexual abuse “with truth, justice, forgiveness, making amends and an evermore resolute commitment to fostering a culture of prevention and protection for the weakest in light of such crimes.”

He also spoke individually in Buenos Aires and Lima with 11 abuse survivors after meetings with other victims in France and Spain this year. According to Vatican statements, the pope heard testimonies of all 11 and was committed to the “creation of safe environments.”

A much larger number of victims had requested to meet with him, but Catholic officials said he could only meet with some because of the hectic schedule during his 12-day visit to the continent. “Naturally, he has to manage this himself, which means making selections, because he doesn’t have much time,” Cardinal Carlos Castillo, the archbishop of Lima, told a local journalist in Peru.

The Vatican’s refusal to explain how it selected the victims who met with the pope has created unease among abuse victims and campaigners. “We don’t know who they met with, who the abusers were or if they were brought to justice,” said Sergio Salinas Giordano, the global director of Ending Clergy Abuse, an international survivors’ group.

Ana María Quispe, 30, was among the abuse survivors who was not invited to meet the pope on this visit.

She has previously accused Leo, when he was a bishop in Chiclayo, Peru, of allowing a priest who she said abused her as a child to continue in his role amid an official inquiry. A New York Times investigation in 2025 uncovered images that showed the priest participating publicly in Mass during the inquiry, contradicting the Church’s announcement that he had been suspended.

Ms. Quispe said she rejected the presentation of the pope as an advocate for abuse victims. “It outrages me; it even disgusts me,” she said in an interview.

The Vatican previously said Leo’s investigation into the priest went “beyond the prerequisites” and closed it because of a lack of evidence, citing the civil authorities’ decision to drop the case.

During an interview, Ms. Quispe was teary, her voice breaking frequently. She said the feeling of not being heard by the Church was more painful than the abuse she experienced as a child. “That’s what destroyed me,” she said. She has been seeking a public apology for her case, Ms. Quispe said, as well as reparation payments for all victims and outside oversight of the Church.

Reinaldo Nann, who was the bishop of Caravelí, Peru, from 2017 until 2024 before resigning to marry a woman, said bishops sometimes did not want to punish the priests they oversee.

“Bishops are given an amount of power that can only be equated with feudalism,” Mr. Nann said. Since the Vatican relies on bishops for information about abuse cases, he said, a bishop can stymie an investigation by withholding evidence. “That is a systemic problem,” Mr. Nann said. “I do not expect changes from Pope Leo on that issue.”

The Church under Leo’s predecessors, Pope Benedict XVI and Pope Francis, was notoriously slow to make policy changes. Leo, who is considered a deliberative decision maker, is unlikely to speed up that process, according to Véronique Lecaros, a professor of theology at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru.

“I think he’s very sensitive to the topic,” said Ms. Lecaros, the president of a commission that collected testimony from abuse victims in Lima. But, she added, “he’s not somebody to hurry up.”

Camila Bustamante, one of the survivors who met with the pope, said she expected the Church to have made more progress in financial reparations to victims.

But she remains hopeful, she said, that Leo will eventually act. “He’s been in for a very short amount of time,” she said.

Lucía Cholakian Herrera contributed reporting from Buenos Aires.

item.title: ‘Russian Objects’ Crashed in Poland, Officials Say. Here’s What We Can See.
item.description:
Poland on Friday said three Russian objects, including at least one missile, violated its airspace and crashed onto Polish territory, denouncing the episodes as a likely Russian “provocation.” The incident followed a wave of Russian air attacks in neighboring Ukraine and came as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine’s allies.

“Three objects, Russian objects, violated Polish airspace,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland told reporters in Warsaw, the capital. “They fell on Polish soil. One exploded.”

The Polish authorities said that no one was harmed and that there were no reports of damage.

Security footage verified by The New York Times shows one of the objects making impact near the village of Nowy Lipowiec, in eastern Poland, about 30 miles from the border with Ukraine. Other verified video shows white smoke rising from the landing site of the object in farmland near a wooded area. The local police said the impact had caused a fire but that no injuries had been reported.

Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, Poland’s defense minister, said at a news conference that the authorities had found impacts in three locations near the country’s eastern border with Ukraine. The one in Nowy Lipowiec, he said, involved “a missile that violated Polish airspace and was located at that site.”

Marcin Kierwinski, Poland’s interior minister, said on social media that residents had received mobile alerts about the airspace violations. Air-raid sirens blared early Friday in the eastern city of Lublin, north of the crash sites.

It was not immediately clear whether the three objects were drones or missiles, debris resulting from the interception of such objects, or a combination of both.

Still, Mr. Tusk described the incident as “another installment of the Russian escalation.” The objects landed as the coalition of the willing, a group of over 30 countries supporting Ukraine, was carrying out scheduled military exercises in Poland.

“It seems we’re dealing with an intentional provocation,” Mr. Tusk said. It was “no coincidence,” he added, that the objects “fell near the site of coalition military exercises, supported by Polish troops.”

Polish officials said that the coalition was carrying out exercises on Friday in Nowa Deba, roughly 20 miles from one of the three crash sites, and that several foreign defense officials were present. The exercises, led by France and Britain, involve forces from 11 countries, last two weeks and are scheduled to end on Sunday.

Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary general, said that jets from the defensive alliance had been deployed in response to the latest incident. “This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” he said on social media.

Russia did not immediately comment on the episode.

Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, a Polish military commander, said at the news conference that it was difficult to tell from radar imagery alone what the three objects were. But they were very fast, suggesting they were cruise missiles or jet-powered drones, he said.

Mr. Kosiniak-Kamysz, the defense minister, said that the first alerts were activated at 1:40 a.m. “Polish F-16s, Swedish Gripens, a Saab reconnaissance aircraft and a Dutch MRTT aerial refueling aircraft took part in the operation,” he said on social media.

In the years since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, drones have routinely intruded into NATO airspace, and it was not the first time that the war in Ukraine spilled over Poland’s border.

In July, a Russian missile crashed in Poland during an overnight assault on neighboring Ukraine, according to NATO. In 2022, an air defense missile that Ukraine had launched accidentally landed on Polish soil.

While Mr. Tusk said on Friday that he was being “cautious” in his wording, he said that “we know for sure that what fell on Polish soil came from Russia.”

The incident came during a large-scale Russian missile and drone assault against Ukraine early Friday that targeted Ukrainian energy and transportation infrastructure; struck bridges in Kyiv, the capital; and caused emergency power blackouts in several regions.

Lara Jakes, Marc Santora and Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting.

item.title: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
item.description:
Iraqi security forces were deployed on Friday in territory long controlled by the country’s most powerful Iran-backed militia, handing Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government a symbolic victory after he had threatened to dislodge the armed group.

Military and police units entered Jarf al-Sakhar, a sprawling area southwest of Baghdad, for the first time in more than a decade, the prime minister’s office said. The militia, Kataib Hezbollah, has dominated the area for years.

But it was unclear whether the group would withdraw, a crucial factor in determining whether the government can claw back power from the dozens of militias that operate in Iraq outside of its control.

Mr. al-Zaidi took office six months ago, at a time when Iraq has come under increasing pressure from the Trump administration to disarm the Iran-backed groups. He has promised to dismantle the militias by June 30, 2027.

The prime minister is moving quickly to try to gain control of the area because of concerns that fighting between Washington and Tehran could intensify soon, according to an official briefed on the negotiations between the government and Kataib Hezbollah to avoid an armed confrontation. Mr. al-Zaidi wanted to limit the group’s ability to join any return to all-out war, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

The Iraqi government had set a deadline of Friday for Kataib Hezbollah’s forces to leave the area after a government inquiry said it had corroborated intelligence reports that the group was involved in oil smuggling and pipeline tampering in the area. Mr. al-Zaidi dismissed nine security and administrative officials and ordered the armed forces into Jarf al-Sakhar. A deal was agreed before the deadline expired.

The contours of the agreement between the government and Kataib Hezbollah were still being finalized, but the deployment did not appear to be a full takeover of the area. It was unclear whether the group would be forced out entirely and whether its activities, which analysts say include arms smuggling and weapons production, would be significantly curtailed.

A plan outlined by the prime minister’s office called for an Iraqi army brigade and a federal police brigade to be deployed alongside paramilitary groups that operate under a grouping known as the Popular Mobilization Forces. The grouping is technically under the authority of Iraq’s national security forces but some militias operate with a large degree of independence and have deep ties with Kataib Hezbollah. Those links could allow the group to retain influence over strategic areas in Jarf al-Sakhar.

Mr. al-Zaidi said in an address to the Iraqi security units that were deployed on Friday that “everyone will integrate into the armed forces under one banner and one command and one law,” adding that there would be “no weapon outside the authority of the state.”

The arrangement could still allow Kataib Hezbollah to retain influence through state-aligned factions that have longstanding ties to the group, according to Lahib Higel, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group. Even so, she said, the arrival of army and police units represented real progress.

“Zaidi will still be able to sell this as a success — which it is, considering that no other prime minister has even been able to enter this location,” Ms. Higel said.

Iraq, like Iran, has a majority Shiite Muslim population. Iran-backed Shiite militias seized control of Jarf al-Sakhar from the Islamic State in 2014, after the jihadist group had swept across Iraq and captured more than a third of it. Local authorities renamed the area Jarf al-Nasr, or Bank of Victory. The fighting displaced thousands of its mostly Sunni residents, and militia forces have prevented many of them from returning.

The area has since become a largely closed military zone dominated by Kataib Hezbollah. The U.S. military said in 2020 that the group maintained heavy-rocket storage and propellant-production facilities there.

Iraqi political and militia leaders had intervened to avoid a confrontation between the government and Kataib Hezbollah. Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s elite Quds Force — an arm of its military that arms and trains militias across the Middle East — traveled to Baghdad to help mediate the standoff, according to the official briefed on the talks and an Iraqi official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions.

Mr. Qaani’s role underscored the limits of the Iraqi prime minister’s effort to curb groups closely aligned with Tehran, analysts said.

“If Kataib Hezbollah leaves Jarf al-Sakhar voluntarily, it is a modest victory for the prime minister, but ultimately, one that was facilitated by the Iranians,” said Victoria Taylor, director of the Iraq Initiative at the Atlantic Council and a former State Department official.

item.title: The War Is Ravaging Ukraine’s Wildlife, Too
item.description:
The remains of dolphins and porpoises have been washing up on Ukraine’s shores.

Fires started by drone debris have burned thousands of acres of forest habitat.

Some animals hurt in the war have been rescued. Most have not been so lucky.

Supported by

Visuals and Text by Nicole Tung

Nicole Tung spent three weeks in Ukraine talking to scientists, park rangers, veterinarians and others about the war’s effects on wildlife and photographing examples of the damage.

The devastating human toll from Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, is well known. But it has also been a catastrophe for the country’s wildlife.

Ukraine is home to an estimated 70,000 plant and animal species, some of them rare and found nowhere else. Its landscapes stretch from ancient pine forests and vast steppes to sprawling wetlands. Though it has less than 6 percent of Europe’s land mass, Ukraine accounts for 35 percent of its biodiversity, according to the Convention on Biological Diversity and the United Nations Development Program.

Millions of livestock are known to have been killed in the war, but the number of wild animals destroyed is impossible to track with any precision. Some of the suffering, though, is plain to see.

Birds, deer, foxes and other animals are often caught in thousands of miles of anti-drone netting installed over roads in Ukraine’s war-ravaged eastern Donbas region, or in webs formed by the hair-thin fiber-optic cables used to operate certain kinds of drones. Only a lucky few of these animals are rescued.

Across the country, fires — started by artillery strikes, incendiary weapons, land mines and debris from shot-down drones — have gutted habitats and displacing wildlife.

“It will take several decades to restore all the damage that has been done,” said Serhiy Premachyuk, director of the Sviati Hory National Park in the Donbas, where fires from the fighting have charred thousands of acres.

Fires sparked by combat have also struck the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, the site of the 1986 nuclear meltdown, posing the unique additional danger that radioactive particles left from the disaster could become airborne in the smoke. In early May, according to official reports, two drones were shot down and crashed in the area, igniting fires in the dry vegetation. Thousands of acres burned.

Days later, a baby moose that had fled the fires lay on a small operating table in a nearby safari park. Veterinarians cut dead tissue away from its burned hooves.

With the government focused on the war, a loose network of rangers, veterinarians, conservationists, volunteers and sanctuaries has emerged to try to rescue wildlife. Some treat wounded birds and foxes; others have taken in lions, bears and primates displaced from zoos near the front or rescued from private homes. Ecological parks have become refuges for creatures brought in with wounds and trauma.

UAnimals, one of Ukraine’s largest animal welfare organizations, has combined such rescues with efforts to document the environmental destruction, in the hope that it might be used in future prosecutions.

Valentina and Leonid Stoyanov, married veterinarians, often get calls from soldiers who have found injured animals at the front. They have traveled to dangerous places to rescue the creatures, many of which they have nursed back to health and released into the wild.

“Our whole clinic was full of birds,” Valentina Stoyanov recalled of the weeks after an oil spill in the Black Sea this year. “A huge number of them died from that spill, it was a big ecological disaster, and it took a long time to rehabilitate the ones we could save because we had to wait for their feathers to molt,” she said.

The conservation work done by rangers at national parks has been profoundly transformed. It now includes fighting fires, evacuating people and animals and removing unexploded mines. Rangers also collect soil samples and other material to assess the war’s environmental effects.

Across the 750-mile front in eastern Ukraine, the landscape has been drastically changed by trenches, anti-tank ditches, minefields, razor wire and anti-drone netting. All of this disrupts animals’ habitats and migratory patterns, to say nothing of those that become entangled and starve or bleed to death.

Even in areas far from the front — such as Nobel National Park, on part of Ukraine’s border with Belarus — wetlands, forests and lakes are scarred by heavily fortified defense lines. “There are three lines of defense along the border, and many kilometers of razor wire and trenches,” said Volodymyr Dikovytskyi, the park’s director. “It has affected the wildlife greatly here.”

The area has one of the biggest populations of European moose, and more than 20 dead cervids, the family of mammals that includes moose and deer, have been found in the fortifications. Many more are presumed to have died. Before the war, wolves and lynxes were often spotted by rangers. Now those predators have largely disappeared.

From a ranger’s tower overlooking Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park, Ivan Rusev scanned with binoculars, looking for birds. The park’s location on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast has put it in the cross hairs of the fighting, which has driven away many of the migratory birds that feed and nest there.

“Many of them have disappeared, and because other migratory corridors around Ukraine are experiencing similar levels of disturbance, they have not found appropriate nesting grounds,” said Dr. Rusev, 67, a biologist specializing in wetland ecology who leads the park’s research department.

He has also warned for years about the war’s effects on dolphins, porpoises and other cetaceans.

He estimates that more than 50,000 died in the conflict’s first year alone. Naval activity, oil spills and a dense network of sea mines have affected their habitats and migrations, when not killing them outright. Between May and July, Dr. Rusev and other scientists counted 84 cetacean carcasses along the coastline.

“We see maybe only 5 percent of the deaths, the rest drift to the bottom of the sea,” he said.

On one stretch of beach, yellow-brown foam with an oily odor had washed up. Dr. Rusev said it was from a Russian strike weeks earlier on a tank that stored sunflower oil, more than 60 miles up the shore.

Months before that, an even larger strike — part of a Russian campaign targeting sunflower oil production in the region — caused a spill that killed thousands of birds and untold numbers of aquatic animals, according to Vladyslav Balynskyi, a biologist. Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities have also caused spills in the Black Sea.

Near the eastern city of Kharkiv, not far from the front, hundreds of displaced animals were being sheltered at Feldman Ecopark, a wildlife refuge. In January, a Russian glide bomb struck the park’s aviary, killing 80 percent of the birds. Some criticized the park for keeping animals so close to the fighting, but staff members said there was nowhere else to take them.

Months after the aviary strike, the park was still open to visitors, even as Russian drones had been targeting civilian traffic on a road running through it. As families walked from cage to cage, an occasional explosion sounded in the distance.

In a temporary aviary, birds with missing wings or other injuries — most caused by anti-drone nets — were tended to by the park’s ornithologist. Elsewhere, a rescued fox slept, and a white Bengal tiger lounged in the sun.

As the war drags on, scientists say, it will further degrade biodiversity and the environment’s resilience in the affected areas. “Nature has no borders, and what happens here will affect the rest of the world,” said Olha Matsko, who leads the strategic initiatives department at UAnimals.

Even Ukraine’s national bird, the stork, has not been spared. In wetlands, on farmland and in villages, the birds, which are deeply ingrained in Ukrainian folklore, have lost their nesting sites.

Tetiana Burianova contributed reporting.

item.title: Britain and Brussels Have Begun a Brexit Rollback. How Far Will It Go?
item.description:
Ten years ago, when the Brexit vote triggered a major rupture between the United Kingdom and the European Union, Donald Trump hailed the decision as a great victory.

These days, President Trump’s policies, along with an aggressive Russia and an economically dominant China, are helping bring Europe and Britain back together.

Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, has made clear that he wants to pursue a much closer relationship with the 27-nation bloc as Russian aggression in Ukraine underscores the need for European solidarity and Mr. Trump calls into question eight decades of American economic, political and security support.

On Friday, the prime minister took concrete steps toward that goal, knocking down some pieces of the Brexit agreement that walled Britain off from its neighbors.

Under plans he announced in Brussels, many trade barriers on food and agricultural products will be cut. Regulations on emissions will be linked. And 100,000 young people in Britain, along with an equal number in Europe, will again have the freedom to work, live and study for up to three years on either side of the English Channel.

The changes will make trade easier for farmers and retailers, travel easier for students, and regulatory compliance easier for companies. At times in the last decade, they were almost unthinkable amid the rancor of the Britain-Europe political divorce.

Mr. Burnham wants to go even further.

On Friday, he and the European Union’s two top leaders agreed to conduct what he described as a yearlong “brainstorm” about what a deeper relationship with the European Union might look like.

“Incremental steps only take you so far,” Mr. Burnham said.

Brexit damaged the British economy, and its continuing cost to businesses and economic growth helped turn a majority of the public against it. But the geopolitical backdrop has played a vital role in the debate.

The postwar world order has been upended by Mr. Trump’s policies, which have come alongside China’s continued economic rise and Russia’s territorial aggression. In a world that looks increasingly hostile, Britain and Europe have been left looking for close friends. And as the trans-Atlantic relationship ruptures, they have found one another again.

“London has increasingly given up on its post-Brexit great trans-Atlantic hopes that Washington would give us a free trade deal and a new lease of life to the special relationship,” said David Lammy, a member of parliament and former deputy prime minister in Britain.

To many foreign policy veterans in Britain, Mr. Trump has spent the first two years of his second administration making it more and more difficult for Britain to feel special. His trade war dragged its already sluggish economy. His relative indifference toward NATO has upended global security. His friendliness with Vladimir Putin has come as a shock.

The same challenges have rocked Europe, another close U.S. ally, and Mr. Trump’s threat to take over Greenland drove home the deterioration. Europe has been looking for alternatives — striking deals with Canada, Australia, Indonesia and Latin American countries.

And as middle powers unite, Europe and Britain have been creeping closer.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Union’s executive arm, suggested that Europe was willing to discuss a deeper relationship.

“We welcome this brainstorming.” she told Mr. Burnham at the news conference, following his suggestion. “So count on us.”

Britain started on its path toward drawing closer to Brussels last year, under the previous Labour prime minister, Keir Starmer. Friday’s summit delivered detailed decisions on several agenda items that his government had begun.

Mr. Burnham said Friday that his government would introduce a bill into Parliament next week to implement the deal and pledged that “we will not waste any time whatsoever in getting on with implementation, rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago.”

But Mr. Burnham has also been clear that he favors an even more substantial reversal of Brexit after what he called “a decade of drift and division” that has left his country poorer and weaker. He has promised to present options for changes to the long-term relationship to the British public in the months to come, while insisting that any final decision would only take place after the next general election, which must be held by 2029.

The prospect of another fierce debate over Britain’s place in Europe is already roiling politics in the United Kingdom, where Mr. Burnham’s rivals have accused him of going back on a Labour promise not to re-litigate the public’s decision in 2016. And in Europe, it is unclear how high support for a drastically closer relationship will be after a series of elections next year.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative Party leader, said this week that the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is.” Nigel Farage, an architect of Brexit and leader of the populist Reform U.K. Party, said Mr. Burnham wanted “to be part of a globalist governmental structure, as opposed to the nation state democracy.”

Still, Mr. Farage acknowledged Brexit had not gone well. “Yes, of course, we cocked things up, but that wasn’t the fault of Brexit — that was the fault of the government not getting it right,” he said in an interview with The Times of London.

Britain remains far from actually rejoining the 27-nation bloc. It took nearly five years for the nation to exit the union, and reversing that would be a complicated and contested process.

“We have seen an improvement in the relationship,” said Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive of the European Policy Centre, a think tank. “But it has been a slow improvement, because a lot of trust has been lost.”

At the same time, deeper ties seem increasingly urgent.

“Brexit has not been good for the U.K. economy — and meanwhile, the trans-Atlantic situation has gone from bad to worse,” said Rebecca Christie, a senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel.

Mr. Trump hammered that point home when he met this week with Presidents Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and Xi Jinping of China, two autocrats whom he described as his friends. Afterward, Mr. Trump called European and British officials and reiterated that the war in Ukraine was costing lives and money.

Europe views the outcome in Ukraine as vital to its security and has been nervously watching as Mr. Trump takes an often-sympathetic tone toward Mr. Putin and an often-hostile one toward President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

Russia is another factor pushing Europe and Britain closer, with both worrying that Mr. Putin’s ambitions do not end in Ukraine. They are also motivated by an economically ascendant China, which is churning out solar panels, electric cars and cutting-edge artificial intelligence models, threatening European industries.

In remarks on Friday, Mr. Burnham accused Russia of spending the last 15 years trying to break apart “the cohesion of like-minded countries and particularly the E.U.” He said that Russia’s efforts were “designed to weaken our ability to stop them in terms of what they were seeking to do” in Ukraine.

“We are going to have to work in a different way to make the next decade different,” Mr. Burnham said. “That will depend upon closer cooperation.”

António Costa, the president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, prompted a ripple of laughter as he joked about how far Britain, and its prime minister, might be willing to rebuild ties with Europe.

“Dear Andy, welcome to Brussels,” Mr. Costa said. “You are always welcome in the European Union.”

item.title: In France’s Angry Autumn, TV News Channels Are Accused of Stirring the Pot
item.description:
When France erupted in nationwide protests last month, the country’s 24-hour television news channels pulled out a well-worn playbook: dramatic footage of billowing tear gas, burning cars, shattered store windows and violent street clashes, amplified by sometimes strident on-air commentary.

Now, two of the main channels, CNews and BFM TV, are under fire themselves, accused of fueling France’s autumn of discontent.

More than a million people signed a petition demanding that the French government revoke the broadcasting license of CNews, citing what they called its right-wing propaganda and racist language, content that regulators have defined as incitement to racial hatred.

At BFM TV, 160 staff members rebelled against what they characterized as a rightward “drift of opinions” expressed on air, saying in a letter to the channel’s bosses that they were ashamed to work there.

A camera crew from BFM TV was attacked by a crowd this month while covering a protest in Lyon, weeks after another crew was accosted at a memorial service for a young Black man killed by a white gunman in a working-class suburb of Paris. The city’s mayor, Ali Rabeh, put the blame for the violence squarely on the news channels, saying that they have poisoned viewers and polarized the political debate.

“It’s what people watch all day long,” said Mr. Rabeh, a left-wing politician whose parents immigrated to France from Morocco in the 1960s and who says the attack traumatized his racially diverse town, Trappes.

Neither CNews nor BFM TV responded to multiple email requests and calls for comment, but both have previously rejected charges of fomenting racially motivated violence. CNews said in a public statement about the petition that “everyone is free to criticize CNews and to challenge its editorial choices,” but that “calling for the elimination of a channel raises a fundamental question regarding pluralism and freedom of the press.”

Speaking to the French paper Le Parisien, the director of BFM TV, Fabien Namias, said his channel offered a platform to people across the political spectrum. “Hatred, racism, exclusion and division are foreign to BFM TV,” he said.

On a recent Sunday, however, two guests on the channel erroneously asserted a direct link between immigration and delinquent behavior in the protests. Last week, a commentator on CNews described Paris as a victim of “migratory submersion,” citing a plan to convert a building into a temporary homeless shelter.

Mr. Rabeh accused the channels of normalizing anti-Muslim language by giving platforms to certain far-right politicians and commentators. He said he wanted to change French law to make it harder for billionaires to own media properties, and to bolster protections for journalists who object to the political tilt of their employers. Cable news channels in the United States, Mr. Rabeh said, offered a troubling precedent.

“There are things that have to change fundamentally,” he said, “to guarantee the freedom of our journalists, to avoid an American-style drift.”

The ratings for France’s news channels are modest relative to Fox News in the United States, to which CNews is often likened because of a similar approach to culture-war issues. While Fox sometimes beats the American broadcast networks in prime-time ratings, France’s news channels have a fraction of the ratings of the leading French commercial broadcaster, TF1.

Still, their viewership has risen over the two months of student-led protests, which they have covered wall to wall. BFM TV reached an aggregate audience of 50.9 million people in October, according to Médiamétrie, a market research company, while CNews reached 44.7 million people. France’s population is roughly 70 million.

With audiences like that, these channels are destined to play an influential — critics say, divisive — role in France’s presidential election next spring. The campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron is unfolding against a combustible backdrop of social unrest, rising populism on the right and left, and fears of additional racially motivated attacks, as officials described the one in Trappes.

“The wind has shifted,” said Samuel Bouron, an expert in media at Paris Dauphine University. “It has put CNews and BFM on the defensive, and these networks are now being called upon to explain themselves, at least regarding how they shape public debates and how they regulate hate speech.”

CNews, which embraces its identity as a French Fox News, has been sanctioned or warned 20 times by France’s broadcast regulator since 2019, six times this year alone. Among the violations: airing statements that incite racial hatred, failing to offer a diversity of views and over-promoting the far right.

Still, France’s National Assembly declined to act on the petition to revoke the channel’s license, saying it was not the job of lawmakers to force a TV channel off the air. Instead, it has scheduled a debate on free speech. CNews noted that more than million signatures is far from a majority of French people.

For some critics, the challenge posed by these channels is as much about money as politics. CNews is owned by a French billionaire and media mogul, Vincent Bolloré; BFM TV, by a French-Lebanese shipping tycoon, Rodolphe Saadé. Critics said the concentration of media properties in the hands of such wealthy owners made them less accountable and more apt to reflect the politics of their proprietors.

Neither man describes himself as politically right-wing, though the output of all of Mr. Bolloré’s media holdings has a conservative angle. In testimony before the National Assembly in March, he described himself as a “Christian democrat,” without an ideological agenda.

Mr. Saadé, who is close to Mr. Macron, a centrist, told lawmakers in 2025 that he does not interfere in the editorial decisions of his holdings. That year, he visited President Trump at the White House, pledging to invest $20 billion in American ports.

BFM TV, which was spun out of an FM radio station, offers a more straight-news diet than the openly political CNews. But in August, BFM TV poached Sonia Mabrouk, a Tunisian-born French journalist, from CNews, where she had developed a reputation for interviewing far-right political figures. Ms. Mabrouk brought that specialty to BFM TV, to the chagrin of many of her new colleagues, who believed that such figures should not get that much airtime, according to two people who work there.

She did not reply to a request for comment.

Some analysts said the rightward creep of BFM TV reflected a recognition that Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far-right party, National Rally, is riding high in the polls and has a plausible path to the presidency. (The party has never entirely disavowed its founder, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and many of its candidates in recent parliamentary elections made racist or antisemitic remarks.)

“It’s not because of ideology; it’s because of interests,” said Alexis Lévrier, a media historian at the University of Reims. “They are people who have finally come to terms with the idea of a probable victory for the National Rally and show signs of compatibility with the extreme right.”

People who work for BFM TV suggest another motive: costs. Fielding a panel of talking heads is cheaper than paying for reporting in the field. The problems begin when those panels feature far-right politicians or commentators whose statements can be both inflammatory and wrong.

Thomas Leonetti, a technician at BFM TV who signed the letter of protest to the channel’s management, said he and his colleagues recognized that they had “a societal responsibility. We work at this channel, but we are also citizens and we realize the impact that such words can have in the public debate.”

“Of course,” Mr. Leonetti added, “we feel shame and embarrassment to say that we work at BFM TV today.”

Giulia Imbert and Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: On the Trail With Spain’s Prime Minister, as He Tries to Pull Out a Win
item.description:
Pedro Sánchez knows what to do to keep his position.

“I always use elbows,” Mr. Sánchez, the prime minister of Spain, said with a laugh in the corner of a locker room as he used lessons learned from his time as a youth basketball player to describe his political game.

It was minutes before a Socialist Party rally in southeastern Spain — in a packed gym fitted with basketball hoops — and a dozen days before national elections on Nov. 29. Polls suggest Mr. Sánchez, Europe’s most prominent left-wing leader, will lose after eight years in charge.

But Mr. Sánchez, known as a political survivor, appeared to relish the idea of being written off once again by the conservatives who are favored. “That is good for me,” he said in a pre-rally interview, looking relaxed in a black mock turtleneck. “It’s a good tactic because at the end of the day, they underestimate me.”

Mr. Sánchez, 54, has beaten the odds in the past, but this time, they are stacked against him.

Outside Spain, he has become a hero to the global left by resisting President Trump, welcoming migrants and denouncing what his government called Israel’s genocide in Gaza, a term rejected by Israel. Under Mr. Sánchez’s leadership, Spain has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing economies and one of its most prolific users of renewable energy. He said that he had put Spain “more in the conversation.”

Yet within Spain, many have had it with him. He has become an increasingly polarizing figure after years of corruption scandals in his inner circle, a national electricity blackout in 2025 and a migration crisis this summer in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

He tried to capitalize on left-wing frustration over spiraling rents by calling for early elections and making the issue his own. But a horrific train crash stalled the momentum that polls showed he was building, shifted voters’ attention and raised unsettling questions about his maintenance of the country’s infrastructure.

Even the online chess matches he plays to relax between campaign events are not going his way. His score of 700 on chess.com — among “the lowest,” he conceded — means his king is often felled.

For most of his career, it has been a different story. Those spurned by Mr. Sánchez, a highly disciplined campaigner, say his chiseled features and abundant charm mask a ruthless political instinct.

He mostly shrugged off regular attacks from Mr. Trump, using them to bolster his left-wing support. He joked that despite the American president “saying all these mean things about me,” Mr. Trump talked to him only about golf when they met in private. “It was weird,” he said with a laugh. The White House declined to comment.

Even Mr. Sánchez’s enemies do not believe the polls. They are traumatized by his previous comebacks, including in 2023, when he managed to assemble a governing coalition despite his party not winning the most votes.

To hear Mr. Sánchez tell it, winning has never been more important. Polling suggests that the conservative Popular Party is likely to take office after the election, in a coalition for the first time with the far-right Vox party.

“The danger is that the last time that the far right was in office in my country was during the dictatorship,” Mr. Sánchez said, suggesting that a coalition of mainstream conservatives and far-right forces risked sending Spain back to the authoritarian rule of Francisco Franco, who died in 1975. Alluding to the Spanish Civil War that installed Franco, he added, “we had of course all these terrible situations in the past.”

For Mr. Sánchez’s enemies, this is a classic stunt by a prime minister whom they portray as the primary cause of Spanish social divisions. They see his use of civil war imagery — he recorded a political ad in front of Pablo Picasso’s “Guernica,” which depicts the horrors of the war — as inflammatory.

“Less civil war, less hatred among Spaniards, less garbage from a century ago,” Santiago Abascal, the leader of Vox, who has called Mr. Sánchez a “dictator,” “traitor” and worse, said at a rally in the Canary Islands on Tuesday.

Mr. Sánchez equates Vox — which is anti-immigrant, nationalist and has challenged Spain’s acceptance of L.G.B.T.Q. rights — with the mainstream conservative Popular Party.

“Today,” he said, “they are more or less the same.”

His intention is to use the possibility of a union between Vox and Popular Party to mobilize his left-wing base — and to attract supporters of far-left parties because they think he is their only shot of averting a right-wing government.

But Mr. Sánchez also needs to peel back Spain’s exasperated centrist voters by seeming more moderate.

“This is a real referendum in favor of good politics,” Mr. Sánchez said from the stump on Tuesday night in Albacete in southeastern Spain. “And against incivility.”

The event capped a busy couple of days during which I shadowed Mr. Sánchez on the campaign trail, including in the Palace of Moncloa, the seat of the Spanish prime minister.

I ate churros with his ministers at a weekly closed-door breakfast, and caught Mr. Sánchez joking with his aides about a right-wing media conspiracy that depicted him as possessing secret tapes to drop on the opposition before Election Day. During a visit from Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fresh off his own comeback election victory, I stood with Mr. Sánchez on Moncloa’s steps as we watched the Brazilian leader delay the departure of their motorcades so he could shoot a video under the branches of a 600-year-old olive tree.

Mr. Lula had come to energize Mr. Sánchez’s campaign. The two leaders drove into central Madrid to film a conversation that had the vibe of a mutual admiration society. The Sánchez campaign quickly chopped it up into social media clips to motivate left-wing supporters.

On the sidelines, André Janones, the architect of Mr. Lula’s come-from-behind victory, applauded as Mr. Lula signed Mr. Sánchez’s red “Power of the People” campaign T-shirts. “Now, it is Spain’s turn to keep this momentum going,” he told me. And since Europe is so barren of left-wing leaders, he said, a “much greater responsibility” fell on Mr. Sánchez.

The tougher assignment for Mr. Sánchez involves bringing moderates back into the fold.

To reach them, he has replaced his far-left deputy prime minister with a more moderate economist, and taken to waving Spanish flags, long a conservative symbol, at rallies. On Tuesday evening, he dropped by the studios of Telecinco, a popular television network seen as lukewarm to the Spanish left.

Before his interview, Mr. Sánchez oozed confidence, talking with one executive, Francisco Moreno, about how he used to play basketball in Converse sneakers.

But when the interview began, the reporter pushed hard on Mr. Sánchez’s political reversals — “Evolutions,” the prime minister called them — and asked tough questions about railway maintenance and Mr. Sánchez’s decision to take a vacation during a migration crisis. Mr. Sánchez bristled after the interviewer rushed his answers so they had more time to discuss corruption scandals involving the prime minister’s associates.

“You get to speak,” Mr. Sánchez snapped. “I have the right to speak, too.”

When Mr. Sánchez walked out, his lips tightened around a forced-seeming smile. He again shook hands with Mr. Moreno and left. “The way television interviews should be,” Mr. Moreno said as he stepped into an elevator.

The next morning in a Moncloa breakfast room adorned with abstract Spanish art, Mr. Sánchez’s ministers sipped coffee from gold-rimmed cups emblazoned with the Spanish coat of arms and said their boss acquitted himself well, considering the forum. Several picked up where Mr. Sánchez had left off.

“Europe needs a strong progressive voice that continues to believe in European values,” said José Manuel Albares, the foreign minister, between bites of a Spanish pastry. Other members of the government said that they felt a sense of momentum.

They were also trying to create it. Minutes later they joined Mr. Sánchez in a room across the hall where they increased the minimum wage and raised salaries for public servants.

Later that night in the locker room, Mr. Sánchez, again in a good mood, stuck with his basketball metaphors. He said “you have to deliver” in the short time one had the ball, something he suggested other left-wing leaders could learn.

Moments later it was time to deliver again. He entered the packed gym, as supporters waved Socialist, Spanish, European and Pride flags. They cheered his litany of accomplishments and hissed at the mention of his right-wing opponents.

“Sánchez won us all over,” Pedro Arnas, 68, said after the event. But out in the country, he said, “It’s going to be tough.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting.
